catalog_citation: Ruffing, Katherine. 2013. A Grammatical Description of Personal Pronoun Use in Uda. Senior essay, Department of Linguistics, Yale University (advisor Dennis Storoshenko), 41 pp. Open PDF: https://ling.yale.edu/media/330/download?inline (Glottolog ref 557252).…
catalog_locator: Ruffing 2013, p. 8 (PDF page 8; printed page number 8), opening paragraph of the tone subsection (3.2) that follows 3.1 Phonetic Inventory. Supporting: Connell…
catalog_quote: Uda is a tonal language, meaning that it uses pitch over syllables to make both lexical and grammatical distinctions. Uda has five phonetic tones. Three of the tones are level tones. These include the high tone, low tone and the downstepped high tone. In addition, Uda has two contour tones. These are the falling tone (combination of a high tone then low tone) and a rising tone (combination of a low tone then high tone.) Though tone is not incorporated in the proposed Uda orthography, it can be represented for clarity, and will be represented where significant in this paper, using the orthographic conventions of other Lower Cross languages.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere. Uda is described as a tone language with H, L, downstepped H, falling (HL) and rising (LH) tones used for lexical and grammatical distinctions; the essay is silent on stress or any other prominence. At the family level Connell (1994: 10) states that all Lower Cross languages have two tones plus contrastive downstep, and (1994: 12) that tonal systems 'appear to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress' but that this has been investigated only for Obolo (Faraclas 1984b) — not for Uda.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Ruffing (p. 5) notes village-level dialect variation 'largely phonological in nature' without detail; Connell (1994: 12) flags uninvestigated phrase-level stress interaction across the group.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexical and grammatical); Ruffing's data are elicited citation forms and short sentences from two educated bilingual (Uda/Ibibio/English) consultants during a four-week CoLang 2012 practicum. Connell's phrasal-stress remark is about the phrase, not the word, and about the group, not Uda specifically. The source is an undergraduate senior essay, not a peer-reviewed description, hence medium confidence.
new_statements.identity_note: Ruffing 2013 describes the Uda of Mbo LGA, Akwa Ibom (twelve villages, largest Ibaka-Uda), i.e. udaa1238 itself; consultants are two educated Uda/Ibibio/English trilinguals and no single village dialect is singled out (p. 5 notes phonological variation among villages). Ruffing places Uda in an 'Obolo language group' whereas Glottolog puts Enwang-Uda (enwa1244) under Oroic; Connell 1994: 12 groups Enwang and Uda together on a shared *b > v development. Connell 1994's tone statement is about the whole Lower Cross group (19 varieties incl. Uda), not Uda alone.

sources.note: Nothing about stress anywhere in the essay (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence: no hits). Sec. 3 Phonetics and 4 Phonology (pp. 7-13) cover segments, tone (§3.2, p. 8: 'Uda is a tonal language.. five phonetic tones': H, L, downstepped H, falling, rising) and syllable structure (§4.5) with no mention of stress or prominence. Data from two consultants (Chris Abasi Eyo, Mfon Asanaenyi) at CoLang 2012, Univ. of Kansas; p. 5 notes village-dialect variation is 'largely phonological'.
